title: Electrician CRM: 7 Tools Compared by Shop Size
html:
An electrician CRM should record every lead, estimate and follow-up in one place. Start with a free sales CRM or a field service app that tracks customers, and add electrician CRM automation once follow-ups start slipping. Published plans here run from free to $69 per seat a month. Three vendors publish no price, so you must ask for a quote.

An electrician CRM has one job: make sure no estimate goes cold. Electrical work is quote-heavy. A panel upgrade or a rewire often needs a site visit, a written estimate and two follow-up calls before the customer signs. This guide compares seven tools by shop size, with the price each vendor publishes and one real limit for each.

Some of these tools are general CRMs and some are field service apps with customer records built in. They solve different problems, so the guide groups them that way.

Which electrician CRM is free to start?

HubSpot and Zoho both list a free CRM tier, so an electrician can track leads for nothing before paying for anything.

  • HubSpot CRM: a general sales CRM with a free tier. The vendor lists it as free for up to 2 users with no credit card. Limit: the free tier holds 1,000 contacts. The paid Starter plan is $20 per seat a month, with a limited-time discount for new customers.
  • Zoho CRM: a sales CRM with a free plan for up to 3 users. Limit: the free plan allows 10 custom email templates, 10 data exports and 5,000 API calls a day. Paid plans are priced per user, and the page shows currency by region, so check the vendor for your figure.

A free CRM works well for an owner who sells most jobs personally. You log each lead, set a follow-up date and move the deal through stages. It does not schedule trucks or send invoices, so you still need a way to run the work.

The 1,000 contact cap on HubSpot sounds high. A shop that keeps every past customer and every estimate request can pass it in a few years. Export your list once a quarter so a move to another tool is easy.

Which electrician CRM also runs jobs and invoices?

Jobber, Housecall Pro and Workiz keep customer records next to scheduling, estimates and invoices. That suits an electrician who wants one tool, not two.

  • Jobber: a field service app with customer records, quotes, scheduling and invoicing. The Core plan for one user is $49 a month with no commitment, or $29 a month billed annually. Limit: extra users cost $29 a month each, and card processing is 2.9% plus 30 cents.
  • Housecall Pro: online booking, scheduling and dispatch, estimates, invoicing and review management. Basic is $59 a month billed annually for one user, and Essentials is $149 a month billed annually for five users. Limit: the pricing page does not list a standalone CRM, so confirm how customer history and follow-ups work.
  • Workiz: client management, scheduling, estimates, invoices and QuickBooks integration. Plans are Standard, Pro and Ultimate, each listed as request pricing. Limit: Standard allows 5 automations, and Genius Leads and Genius Scheduling start on Pro.

The all-in-one route saves double entry. A lead from your website becomes a customer, then a job, then an invoice, with no retyping. The cost is that you take on the whole tool, including the parts you do not use.

Housecall Pro lists a 14 day trial with no credit card, and Workiz lists 7 days. Use the trial to log ten real leads and chase each one. A CRM is only as good as the follow-ups it makes easy.

Which electrician CRM suits a team with a sales rep?

A shop with a full-time estimator or sales rep needs pipeline views and contact limits that a job app does not offer. Copper and FieldEdge both fit that case, in different ways.

  • Copper: a paid sales CRM. Basic is $29 per seat a month billed monthly, or $23 billed annually, and holds 2,500 contacts. Professional is $69 monthly or $59 annually for 15,000 contacts. Limit: it stores contacts and deals but does not schedule jobs or invoice customers.
  • FieldEdge: a field service platform with scheduling, dispatching, quotes, service agreements and prospect tracking. Select, Premier and Elite include 2, 4 and 6 mobile app licenses. Limit: prices are request pricing, and prospect tracking is not included on Select.

Copper is a clean fit when the estimator lives in email and calls. FieldEdge fits when the same office also dispatches electricians and sells service agreements. Ask FieldEdge for the Premier price in writing, since that is the lowest plan with prospect tracking.

How do the seven electrician CRM tools compare?

The table puts the published facts side by side so you can see where each tool starts and where it stops.

ToolPublished entry priceUsersMain limit
HubSpot CRMFree, Starter listed at $20 a seat a monthUp to 2 on free1,000 contacts on free
Zoho CRMFree plan, paid prices vary by regionUp to 3 on free10 data exports on free
Copper$23 a seat a month billed annuallyPer seat2,500 contacts on Basic
Jobber$29 a month billed annually, $49 with no commitment1 on CoreExtra users cost $29 a month
Housecall Pro$59 a month billed annually1 on BasicNo standalone CRM listed
WorkizRequest pricingNot shown5 automations on Standard
FieldEdgeRequest pricing2 app licenses on SelectNo prospect tracking on Select

Source: the vendor's published prices, read in November 2026. Prices exclude tax and card processing fees.

Read the table by role. An owner who sells alone should start free. A shop that wants one system should price Jobber, Housecall Pro or Workiz. A shop with a sales rep should price Copper or FieldEdge.

How should an electrician set up CRM pipeline stages?

Use six stages that match how electrical jobs move: new lead, site visit booked, estimate sent, follow-up, won or lost, and review request.

  1. New lead. Log the source, the job type and the callback time. Source tracking shows which channel pays.
  2. Site visit booked. Move the lead here only when a date is on the calendar.
  3. Estimate sent. Attach the written price and set a follow-up date before you close the screen.
  4. Follow-up. Call after two days and again after a week. Note the reply so the next call starts informed.
  5. Won or lost. Record the reason for every loss. Price, timing and a competitor are the usual answers.
  6. Review request. Ask for a Google review while the work is fresh.

Keep stages few. A pipeline with twelve columns goes stale because no one wants to update it. If a stage never changes what you do next, delete it.

Pay attention to lost reasons after three months. If most losses say price, tighten how you present the estimate. If they say timing, your callback is too slow.

What should an electrician test in a CRM trial?

Test how fast you can answer a new lead, not how pretty the dashboard looks. Speed to the first callback decides many electrical jobs.

  • Capture: send a test lead from your website form and see whether it lands in the CRM without retyping.
  • Reminders: set a follow-up for two days out and confirm your phone alerts you.
  • Mobile use: log a lead from the truck in under a minute, with one hand.
  • Export: download your full list as a file, so you know you can leave.

Give the trial to the person who answers the phone, not only the owner. The office manager will find the slow steps first. If entering a lead takes more than a minute, leads will go unlogged by Friday.

Import your past estimates, too. A CRM full of old quotes lets you call back people who asked for a price last spring and never heard a no.

What does an electrician CRM stack cost per month?

A small electrician stack can cost $0 for the CRM. A job app runs about $29 to $149 a month, using only the published prices above.

  • Solo electrician: HubSpot or Zoho free tier plus a free Google Business Profile. The CRM cost is $0.
  • Two-truck shop: Jobber Core at $29 a month billed annually, plus $29 for a second user, which is $58 a month.
  • Five-person shop: Housecall Pro Essentials at $149 a month billed annually covers five users.
  • Shop with a sales rep: Copper Basic at $23 per seat a month billed annually, or FieldEdge by quote.

These figures cover the software only. Card processing, phone numbers and add-ons sit on top. Compare the total with one average job, and shrink the plan if it costs more than a week of calls.

Plan for the cost of switching, too. Moving customer records and estimates to a new app takes real hours. Pick a tool you can live with for two years so today's price is not a trap later.

What does an electrician CRM not do?

A CRM stores leads. It does not create them, so a full pipeline still depends on search, maps, reviews and ads.

  • Google Business Profile: the free listing that puts an electrical company on Google Maps. Google states that creating a Business Profile and listing your business is free. Limit: it needs fresh photos and review replies to rank near the top.

Pair it with electrician reputation management so the review request in your pipeline turns into stars on the map.

Calls need tracing too. Call tracking and attribution shows which ad or page rang the phone, so your CRM source field holds real answers instead of guesses.

How do you choose an electrician CRM?

Choose an electrician CRM with a three-check filter: fit, cost and setup effort. Run every tool through all three before you pay.

Fit: does it track estimates and follow-up dates, and can you see every lead by source?

Cost: add the plan price, extra seats, add-ons and card fees, then compare the total with one average panel upgrade.

Setup effort: can one person import your customer list and build the pipeline stages in a weekend?

A solo electrician can run on a free HubSpot or Zoho plan and a free Google Business Profile. A three-truck shop with a dispatcher fits Jobber or Housecall Pro. A shop with a sales rep and service agreements should price Copper and FieldEdge side by side.

A CRM does not create demand, so pair it with lead sources. Search ads from Google Ads for electricians and Google Local Services Ads bring calls in.

A site that captures leads feeds the CRM directly. Past leads are worth an email marketing follow-up too.

What is the best CRM for an electrician?

There is no single best, because it depends on how you sell. A solo owner can start with HubSpot or Zoho, which both list a free tier. A shop that wants jobs and invoices in one place should price Jobber, Housecall Pro or Workiz. Test each on real leads.

Is there a free CRM for electricians?

Yes. HubSpot lists a free CRM for up to 2 users with a 1,000 contact limit, and Zoho lists a free plan for up to 3 users. Both are general sales CRMs, so they do not schedule trucks or send invoices. You would pair them with a job app later.

How much does an electrician CRM cost?

Published plans in this guide run from free to $69 per seat a month for Copper Professional. Copper starts at $23 per seat monthly on annual billing, and Jobber Core starts at $29 a month on annual billing. Workiz and FieldEdge publish no prices, so ask each for a written quote.

Do electricians need a CRM if they use job software?

Often not. Jobber, Housecall Pro and Workiz keep customer records next to jobs, so a separate CRM can duplicate your list. Add a sales CRM only when an estimator or sales rep needs pipeline views and contact limits that your job app lacks.

What should an electrician track in a CRM?

Track the lead source, job type, estimate amount, follow-up date and the reason for each lost job. Those five fields show which channel pays, how fast you follow up and where you lose on price. Add a review request step for won jobs.

Can a CRM get an electrician more leads?

No. A CRM organizes leads you already have and helps you follow up faster. New leads come from search, maps, reviews and ads. A free Google Business Profile, a fast website and paid search put your number in front of homeowners first.

How long does it take to set up an electrician CRM?

A free CRM with six pipeline stages takes a few hours to set up and a weekend to fill with your past leads. Field service apps take longer because of price books and templates. Use the trial period to import a real customer list.

Test how fast you can answer a new lead, not how pretty the dashboard looks. Speed to the first callback decides many electrical jobs.
-
Capture:
send a test lead from your website form and see whether it lands in the CRM without retyping.
-
Reminders:
set a follow-up for two days out and confirm your phone alerts you.
-
Mobile use:
log a lead from the truck in under a minute, with one hand.
-
Export:
download your full list as a file, so you know you can leave.
Give the trial to the person who answers the phone, not only the owner. The office manager will find the slow steps first. If entering a lead takes more than a minute, leads will go unlogged by Friday.
Import your past estimates, too. A CRM full of old quotes lets you call back people who asked for a price last spring and never heard a no.
##
What does an electrician CRM stack cost per month?
A small electrician stack can cost $0 for the CRM. A job app runs about $29 to $149 a month, using only the published prices above.
-
Solo electrician:
HubSpot or Zoho free tier plus a free Google Business Profile. The CRM cost is $0.
-
Two-truck shop:
Jobber Core at $29 a month billed annually, plus $29 for a second user, which is $58 a month.
-
Five-person shop:
Housecall Pro Essentials at $149 a month billed annually covers five users.
-
Shop with a sales rep:
Copper Basic at $23 per seat a month billed annually, or FieldEdge by quote.
These figures cover the software only. Card processing, phone numbers and add-ons sit on top. Compare the total with one average job, and shrink the plan if it costs more than a week of calls.
Plan for the cost of switching, too. Moving customer records and estimates to a new app takes real hours. Pick a tool you can live with for two years so today's price is not a trap later.
##
What does an electrician CRM not do?
A CRM stores leads. It does not create them, so a full pipeline still depends on search, maps, reviews and ads.
-
Google Business Profile:
the free listing that puts an electrical company on Google Maps. Google states that creating a Business Profile and listing your business is free. Limit: it needs fresh photos and review replies to rank near the top.
Pair it with electrician reputation management so the review request in your pipeline turns into stars on the map.
Calls need tracing too.
[Call tracking and attribution](/solutions/electrician-call-tracking-attribution/)
shows which ad or page rang the phone, so your CRM source field holds real answers instead of guesses.
##
How do you choose an electrician CRM?
Choose an electrician CRM with a three-check filter: fit, cost and setup effort. Run every tool through all three before you pay.
Fit:
does it track estimates and follow-up dates, and can you see every lead by source?
Cost:
add the plan price, extra seats, add-ons and card fees, then compare the total with one average panel upgrade.
Setup effort:
can one person import your customer list and build the pipeline stages in a weekend?
A solo electrician can run on a free HubSpot or Zoho plan and a free Google Business Profile. A three-truck shop with a dispatcher fits Jobber or Housecall Pro. A shop with a sales rep and service agreements should price Copper and FieldEdge side by side.
A CRM does not create demand, so pair it with lead sources. Search ads from Google Ads for electricians and Google Local Services Ads bring calls in.
A site that captures leads feeds the CRM directly. Past leads are worth an email marketing follow-up too.
###
What is the best CRM for an electrician?
There is no single best, because it depends on how you sell. A solo owner can start with HubSpot or Zoho, which both list a free tier. A shop that wants jobs and invoices in one place should price Jobber, Housecall Pro or Workiz. Test each on real leads.
###
Is there a free CRM for electricians?
Yes. HubSpot lists a free CRM for up to 2 users with a 1,000 contact limit, and Zoho lists a free plan for up to 3 users. Both are general sales CRMs, so they do not schedule trucks or send invoices. You would pair them with a job app later.
###
How much does an electrician CRM cost?
Published plans in this guide run from free to $69 per seat a month for Copper Professional. Copper starts at $23 per seat monthly on annual billing, and Jobber Core starts at $29 a month on annual billing. Workiz and FieldEdge publish no prices, so ask each for a written quote.
###
Do electricians need a CRM if they use job software?
Often not. Jobber, Housecall Pro and Workiz keep customer records next to jobs, so a separate CRM can duplicate your list. Add a sales CRM only when an estimator or sales rep needs pipeline views and contact limits that your job app lacks.
###
What should an electrician track in a CRM?
Track the lead source, job type, estimate amount, follow-up date and the reason for each lost job. Those five fields show which channel pays, how fast you follow up and where you lose on price. Add a review request step for won jobs.
###
Can a CRM get an electrician more leads?
No. A CRM organizes leads you already have and helps you follow up faster. New leads come from search, maps, reviews and ads. A free Google Business Profile, a fast website and paid search put your number in front of homeowners first.
###
How long does it take to set up an electrician CRM?
A free CRM with six pipeline stages takes a few hours to set up and a weekend to fill with your past leads. Field service apps take longer because of price books and templates. Use the trial period to import a real customer list.
